Structure-loss paper

Wildfire structure loss: paper exploration · 2026-10-12

Everything we have tested for the paper, in one place: what makes an urban conflagration (now with the cluster rule on all three records, Lahaina and Waldo Canyon as outside tests, and loss signatures), losses by year 2002–2025 (2026 apart), how concentrated losses are, which fires lose buildings, whether building density raises loss, and mobile homes — each in Carlson 2002–22, our 2002–26 record and CAL FIRE inspections where the data allow.

By Carlo Broderick, NCEAS, UC Santa Barbara · 2026-10-13 13:45 PDT

Four findings so far. An urban conflagration happens when a fire reaches one connected cluster of roughly 90 or more buildings standing within 20 m of each other, in all three records. Buildings destroyed per year roughly tripled between 2008–2016 and 2017–2025, almost all in fires that destroyed 1,000 or more, and leaning on a few disaster years; whether more fires destroy any building, we can't tell. Inside a fire, building density barely changes a building's chance of loss; there is no density threshold. Mobile homes are destroyed somewhat more often than houses in the same fire, much of it explained by density and size.

How to read this page

Each section answers one question; every point and bar explains itself on hover. Use the Plain language / Technical switch at the top for definitions and methods. Tick or untick a line in a key to show or hide it. Under each panel, How this panel was checked lists the rigor checks it passed.

Three full records appear wherever the data allow: Carlson 2002–22 (blue), our 2002–26 record (green) and CAL FIRE inspections (pink). Subsets (fires with 100 or more exposed buildings, the five largest fires removed, fires chosen regardless of loss in 2023–25) are checks on the three full records, not replacements for them. The year 2026 is partial and never sits beside full years.

1. What makes an urban conflagration?

Is 89 buildings a tipping point? We can't tell (added 2026-10-13 21:15 PDT)

Each row is one record. The grey part is where fires almost never burned down 50 or more neighbouring buildings in one patch (chance under 1 in 20). The coloured part is where the chance climbs to 1 in 2: from a block of about 60–70 buildings to about 190–210. The thin lines under each bar show how uncertain those two points are. A true tipping point would make the coloured part very short; it spans about a threefold growth in block size. The test we used earlier to say "no step" would have missed a real step about half the time, and on two records it could not even look at 89, so the honest answer is: we can't tell a sharp step from a steep climb. What we can say: no fire with a block under about 60 buildings burned through, and predicting each fire from the others works better with a gradual climb.Firth logit P(LDC30 ≥ 50) on log10(1 + largest exposed component at 35 m centroid links); P = 5 % and 50 % points with fire-bootstrap ranges (whiskers: lower = 5 % point, upper = 50 % point). Power: M3 sup-LR (step-on-smooth, p24c) critical value from 999 draws under fitted M1; 500 draws under a pure step at 89.1 (P = 0 below, observed rate above). The ψ grid spans the 5th–95th percentile of s, which on the full records ends at 59–62 buildings. LOO: M1 vs pure step M4 (Jeffreys-smoothed rates). How this panel was checked

What a conflagration looks like from the losses: other signatures, and no separate class (added 2026-10-13 13:45 PDT)

Other measures agree with the linked-cluster definition. In our record, 82% of a conflagration's destroyed buildings had a destroyed neighbour within 30 m (other fires 33%); it destroyed 217 buildings per km² of developed land (others 31); losses reached 696 m inside the built-up edge (others 100 m); and 92% of the largest exposed cluster was lost (others 0%). Burn-out of 500 m cells separates less (50% vs 33%). Carlson and CAL FIRE DINS agree. But there is no separate kind of fire: the fires form a continuous fan, with conflagrations at its tip and near-misses (Rice 2007, Hennessey 2020, Lilac 5 2017, Dixie 2021, Carr 2018, Erskine 2016) next to them. Two partly independent axes describe it: how far the loss linked through the town (left–right) and how completely the reached blocks burned (up–down).Signatures on destroyed buildings: S2 share with a destroyed neighbour ≤30 m; S4 destroyed per km² developed area burned; S5a farthest destroyed building from the built-up edge (100 m grid); S6 loss rate in the largest exposed cluster; S3 burn-out share of reached 500 m cells. Medians with fire-bootstrap ranges. Gaussian mixtures (k by BIC) on six signatures, judged by Ashman D on PC1, bootstrap co-assignment and ARI (PA33, pre-registered).

How this panel was checked
  • Signatures measured on the losses after the fire, in all three records; fires with 10+ destroyed only (342 / 417 / 108 fires).
  • Medians, not means (heavy tails); ranges are fire-bootstrap ranges of the conflagration median.
  • Is there a distinct class? Gaussian mixtures on six signatures prefer three groups in every record, but the groups are not separated or not stable: Ashman D 1.07 / 0.87 / 2.03 (pre-registered bar above 2), co-assignment 0.83 / 0.84 / 0.70 (bar 0.8). Verdict in all three: a continuum.
  • Depth inside the built-up edge comes from a 100 m grid, so 100 m is its floor; Carlson points have no footprints.
  • The scatter shows our record; Carlson and DINS give the same fan (PA33 figure p27_2d_view).

The line on the curve: chance of an urban conflagration as clusters grow, in three records (updated 2026-10-13 13:45 PDT)

Each tick is a fire in our record: along the top, the 10 that became urban conflagrations; along the bottom, the rest. Each curve is the fitted chance in one record, with its 95% range shaded. In our 2002–26 record the chance is 2% (0%–4%) at a 50-building cluster, 10% (2%–17%) at 90 and 55% (30%–83%) at 200; Carlson alone gives nearly the same curve. The rise is steep but smooth: the dashed line is where it best separates fires that conflagrated from those that did not. Diamonds are outside fires never used in the fit: Lahaina 2023 and Waldo Canyon 2012 sit above the line, and both conflagrated. Squares are Gatlinburg 2016, Black Forest 2013 and Bastrop 2011: large losses spread through low-density housing, below the line, with no urban conflagration. Subsets (fires with 100 or more exposed buildings, the five largest fires removed, fires chosen regardless of loss in 2023–25) are checks on the three full records, not replacements for them.Firth-penalised logistic regression of conflagration (≥50 destroyed buildings linked within 30 m) on log10(1 + largest connected component of exposed buildings, centroids linked at ≤35 m ≈ 20 m edge gap for the median 159 m² footprint), fitted separately per record; bands = 2.5–97.5th percentiles of 1,000 fire-bootstrap refits. Cut = Youden-optimal threshold on fires with ≥100 exposed (89.1). Circles: exact (Clopper–Pearson) ranges.

Observed share in each size group (our record), 95% rangeEach fire in our record: top = conflagration, bottom = notOutside conflagrations (Lahaina 2023, Waldo Canyon 2012)Big losses below the line (Gatlinburg, Black Forest, Bastrop)
How this panel was checked
  • Three full records, each with its own fitted curve and 95% band (1,000 fire-bootstrap refits): Carlson 361 fires / 8 events; our record 726 / 10; CAL FIRE DINS 445 / 7.
  • Not independent: Carlson fires are part of our record, and the California conflagrations appear in all three.
  • 28 fires in our record have no exposed building on file and are left out; none of them was an urban conflagration.
  • Small n: 10 events in our record (8 in CA, 1 in CO, 1 in OR). Binned shares use exact (Clopper–Pearson) ranges.
  • Out of sample: Lahaina 2023 and Waldo Canyon 2012 were not used for any fit; both sit above the line and conflagrated. Gatlinburg, Black Forest and Bastrop (in Carlson) lost 785–1,517 buildings each yet sit below the line, with no urban conflagration.
  • Smooth rise, not a step: a step added to the smooth logit was not supported (bootstrap p 0.67, fires with 100+ exposed).
  • Exposure is counted inside the final perimeter, which is partly an outcome. With exposure fixed before the fire (buildings within 5 km of ignition) the cluster measure still ranks first (AUC 0.88) but misses Tubbs CA 2017, Camp CA 2018, Glass CA 2020, whose towns lay beyond 5 km.
  • Fires from 2026 enter as fires (no per-year statistic); their outcome is our model's call unless CAL FIRE inspected them.

Chance a fire becomes an urban conflagration, by the size of its largest connected cluster of buildings

An urban conflagration here means 50 or more destroyed buildings joined in one chain: each is no more than 30 m (centre to centre) from another destroyed building in the chain. Not a circle; the chain can run for kilometres. In every record it did not happen unless the fire reached a chain of at least 50 buildings, each about 20 m or less wall to wall from the next; above 200 it is common. Events per record: 8 (Carlson), 10 (ours), 7 (CAL FIRE DINS).Unit = fire; exact binomial 95% ranges. Records as in the panel above.

Two candidate rules, scored on each record

The cluster rule catches every conflagration in every record, with far fewer false alarms than the density rule. In fires chosen regardless of loss (2023–25), only Eaton and Palisades crossed the cluster line, and both conflagrated.Cuts fitted on our record's fires with ≥100 exposed (Youden), then applied unchanged. Caveats: 10 events in our record (8 in CA, 1 in CO, 1 in OR); exposure from the final perimeter is partly an outcome. The held-out 2016–22 fires will test the 'below the line' side (registered before any result).

Where did the growth come from? Destroyed per year in two equal 9-year periods, by size of fire

Buildings destroyed per year rose about ×3.3 between 2008–2016 and 2017–2025 in situation reports (95% range 1.4–6.3) and ×2.9 (1.2–6.1) between 2003–2011 and 2012–2020 in ICS-209-PLUS. The rise is in fires that destroyed 1,000 or more (1,057 → 7,785 a year); fires with 1–9 and 10–99 destroyed show no clear change (×1.06 and ×0.96). It leans on a few disaster years: without each period's largest year the rise is ×2.6 (1.1–5.0), and without the two largest ×2.4 (0.9–4.9), where the range includes no change.Ratio of mean annual totals by order-of-magnitude class, later ÷ earlier equal period; 95% ranges from 10,000 year-bootstrap draws (years resampled within each period). 3. How concentrated are losses, and is that changing?

Concentration curve: share of all losses held by the most destructive fires

Fires ranked from most to least destructive, full years only. In the situation reports (2007–25) the top 1% of loss fires hold 60% of all destroyed buildings, the top 5% hold 83% and the top 10% 90%; ICS-209-PLUS (2002–20) gives 65%, 84% and 90%. Carlson looks less concentrated only because it leaves out fires with 1–9 losses.

How this panel was checked
  • Full years only (2026 left out).
  • Each source on its own fires; the curves are not pooled.
  • Carlson's curve is not comparable: by design it holds no fire with fewer than 10 destroyed.

Did concentration rise? Two equal 9-year periods

Losses became more unequal by the Gini coefficient: +8 points (+2 to +12) in situation reports and +10 points (+3 to +18) in ICS-209-PLUS. For the top-1% share we can't tell: +18 points (-10 to +38) and +18 points (-6 to +39), ranges that include no change, because the top 1% is only about 11 fires per period and a single disaster year moves it.Top-1% share and Gini of destroyed per loss fire, equal full-year periods; 95% ranges from a year-cluster bootstrap (resample years, keep their fires; 2,000 draws), which carries the dominance of single years.

Between 17% and 29% a year at the typical exposure. Can't tell whether it changed: the odds per decade are 1.07× (0.99–1.16), a range that includes no change and also a small rise. 4. Most fires that reach buildings destroy few or none

Share of fires and of destroyed buildings by size of fire, in the three full records

In every record, fires that destroyed more than 100 buildings are a minority of fires but hold almost all losses: 89% of destroyed buildings in Carlson (27% of fires), 89% in our record (15% of fires) and 95% in CAL FIRE DINS (10% of incidents). Carlson's 0 and 1–9 rows are near empty by design: it maps only fires that destroyed 10 or more. 5. Building density and loss inside a fire

Destroyed, compared with the rest of the same fire

In Carlson and in our full record the ratio stays near 1× up to about 60 neighbours within 100 m; the rise above that rests on few fires (hollow points) and disappears in the Carlson check without mobile-home parks. In the CAL FIRE inspections (31 incidents with variation in loss), buildings with 6-10 neighbours were destroyed 0.72× as often as the rest of their fire (0.54–0.94); above 11-20 neighbours fewer than 10 incidents remain, too few to tell. Subsets (fires with 100 or more exposed buildings, the five largest fires removed, fires chosen regardless of loss in 2023–25) are checks on the three full records, not replacements for them.Observed/expected by n100 bin, expected from each building's own-fire rate (removes between-fire differences); 95% fire-bootstrap ranges; hollow = fewer than 10 fires. Points are offset sideways so the records do not overlap.

How this panel was checked
  • Three full records drawn solid; the Carlson-without-parks line (squares, dashed) is a labelled check on 32 dense fires.
  • Within-fire comparison: each building is compared with its own fire's loss rate, so between-fire differences cancel.
  • Small n: hollow points have fewer than 10 fires and no range is drawn. CAL FIRE has 10 or more fires only in bins 1-2, 3-5, 6-10, 11-20.
  • 95% ranges resample fires (1,000 draws), not buildings.

Is there a step? The jump in the odds of loss at 60 neighbours

A step test asks whether loss jumps at some density, instead of rising smoothly. Here: how much higher the odds of loss are just above 60 neighbours than just below, in the same fire. Every range includes 1 in all three records and in every check: no step that holds up. Carlson's estimates point up, driven by Sayre's mobile-home park.Fixed step at n100 = 60 added to a 4-df spline in log2(1+n100) with fire fixed effects; free-location hinge and step models (ψ grid 1–99.5th percentile, Davies test, AIC vs spline) gave the same verdict.

Where the losses pile up, from sparsest to densest

Walk from the sparsest unit (left) to the densest (right); the line is the share of all losses passed so far. On the dotted diagonal, losses follow exposure; below it, the dense end lost more than its share. Buildings with more than 20 neighbours are 16% of exposed and 16% of destroyed in Carlson; 19% of exposed and 24% of destroyed in our record; 67% of exposed and 81% of destroyed in the CAL FIRE inspections. Without each record's five largest fires (dashed): 14% of exposed and 8% of destroyed; 13% of exposed and 7% of destroyed; 15% of exposed and 5% of destroyed. A handful of conflagrations make density look dangerous.Pooled across fires, so it mixes between- and within-fire differences; the within-fire chart above isolates the latter. Five largest by destroyed: Carlson — Camp, Tubbs, Almeda Drive, Valley, Cedar; 2002–26 — Camp, Eaton, Palisades, Tubbs, Almeda Drive.

6. Mobile homes

How much more often are mobile homes destroyed than houses in the same fire?

In the same fire, a mobile home is destroyed about 1.2 times as often as a single-family home in the CAL FIRE inspections (1.15–1.41; odds 2.4×), 1.4× in Carlson (1.11–2.05) and 1.4× in our record (1.12–1.90). The ratio looks small because in the inspected areas 51% of single-family homes were destroyed too. At the same building size the CAL FIRE gap nearly closes (1.02× (0.95–1.33)). Subsets (fires with 100 or more exposed buildings, the five largest fires removed, fires chosen regardless of loss in 2023–25) are checks on the three full records, not replacements for them.Risk ratio, mobile home (single/double/triple wide) vs single-family residence, stratified by fire (Mantel–Haenszel) or fire-fixed-effects Poisson with covariates; 95% fire-cluster bootstrap.

Mobile homes' share of exposure and of losses

Mobile homes are about one exposed home in ten but a larger share of destroyed homes in every record: 10% → 19% in Carlson, 10% → 14% in our record and 10% → 15% in CAL FIRE DINS; in CAL FIRE fires with 1–9 destroyed, 35%. Parks or density? Mobile homes vs houses at the same density

At the same density, in the CAL FIRE inspections (the one record that types every structure on site) mobile homes in parks are not clearly different from houses (1.14× (0.85–2.46)) and scattered mobile homes riskier than houses (2.36× (2.02–3.02)). In Carlson, parks 2.19× (0.98–4.78) and scattered 1.29× (0.81–1.85); in our record 1.95× (0.93–3.80) and 1.28× (0.89–1.72). Where a range includes 1 we can't tell that group from houses; typing in Carlson and our record finds only a minority of mobile homes, which blurs both.Fire-fixed-effects logit with three classes (park mobile home, scattered mobile home, single-family) and density splines; park = inside a HIFLD mobile-home park radius or a dense mobile-home neighbourhood. Pre-registered H2 (parks riskier at the same density).
